# CSRD Disclosure Requirements Based on Your Double Materiality Assessment

## Overview

Under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), companies only need to provide detailed disclosures for topics that are material. Your double materiality assessment identified three material topics: Climate Change (ESRS E1), Own Workforce (ESRS S1), and Business Conduct (ESRS G1). Non-material topics do not require full standard-level disclosures, though you must document and explain your materiality conclusions.

The following outlines what you must disclose.

---

## 1. Cross-Cutting / General Disclosures (Always Required)

Regardless of materiality outcomes, ESRS 1 and ESRS 2 apply to all companies in scope of CSRD. These are not subject to materiality — they form the mandatory baseline.

### ESRS 1 (General Requirements)
This standard sets out the architecture, principles, and methodology for sustainability reporting. It does not itself contain disclosure requirements but governs how you apply the other standards.

### ESRS 2 (General Disclosures) — Fully Mandatory
You must disclose all requirements under ESRS 2, which covers:

- **Governance (GOV)**: Governance bodies' oversight of sustainability matters, management roles and responsibilities, integration of sustainability in corporate governance
- **Strategy (SBM)**: Business model and value chain description, sustainability strategy and significant groups of stakeholders, material impacts, risks and opportunities and how they interact with strategy and business model
- **Impact, Risk and Opportunity Management (IRO)**: The process used to identify, assess, prioritise and monitor material IROs — including a full description of your double materiality assessment process
- **Metrics and Targets (MT)**: Disclosure of the sustainability-related targets set and performance against those targets

ESRS 2 also requires you to disclose the **list of material sustainability matters** identified through your assessment, and critically, an **explanation of why topics assessed as non-material were excluded**. This means you must document why Pollution (E2), Water (E3), Biodiversity (E4), Circular Economy (E5), Value Chain Workers (S2), Communities (S3), and Consumers/End-users (S4) were determined non-material.

---

## 2. Material Topic Disclosures

For the three topics that came out as material, you must apply the relevant topical ESRS standards. Each topical standard contains a mix of mandatory disclosures and disclosures subject to materiality.

---

### ESRS E1 — Climate Change

This is one of the most demanding ESRS standards. Key disclosure areas include:

**Governance and Strategy**
- Transition plan for climate change mitigation aligned with Paris Agreement / 1.5°C pathway
- Climate-related physical and transition risks and opportunities
- Resilience of business model and strategy under climate scenarios (scenario analysis)
- Integration of climate into overall strategy and financial planning

**Impact, Risk and Opportunity Management**
- Policies for climate change mitigation and adaptation
- Actions and resources allocated to manage climate-related IROs
- Engagement with value chain on climate matters

**Metrics and Targets**
- **Scope 1, 2, and 3 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions** — this is a core mandatory metric; Scope 3 can be phased in for some companies
- GHG removal and storage activities
- GHG intensity metrics
- Energy consumption and mix (renewable vs. non-renewable)
- Climate-related targets, including whether aligned with science-based targets
- Potential financial effects of material climate risks

Note: ESRS E1 includes some of the most prescriptive quantitative requirements in the entire framework, particularly around GHG accounting methodology (aligned with GHG Protocol).

---

### ESRS S1 — Own Workforce

This standard covers your employees and non-employee workers (e.g., contractors working under your direction).

**Governance and Strategy**
- Policies related to your own workforce (e.g., fair wages, health and safety, non-discrimination, working conditions)
- How you engage with your own workforce on material topics

**Impact, Risk and Opportunity Management**
- Processes for identifying and managing impacts on your own workforce
- Remediation processes for identified negative impacts
- Channels for workers to raise concerns

**Metrics and Targets**
- **Headcount data**: total workforce broken down by gender, country, employment type (permanent/temporary, full-time/part-time), non-employees
- **Health and safety**: work-related injuries, ill health, and fatalities (rates and absolute numbers)
- **Work-related health and safety management system** coverage
- **Remuneration**: pay gap metrics (gender pay gap), ratio of CEO pay to median employee pay
- Collective bargaining coverage
- Training and skills development metrics
- Diversity metrics (particularly gender across governance and management levels)
- Cases of discrimination, harassment, and outcomes

Several S1 metrics are mandatory even if the underlying sub-topic might have limited materiality; others apply only where the relevant sub-topic (e.g., remuneration adequacy, work-life balance) is material.

---

### ESRS G1 — Business Conduct

This standard covers ethics, anti-corruption, anti-bribery, lobbying, supplier relationships, and payment practices.

**Governance and Strategy**
- Corporate culture and conduct policies (code of conduct, anti-corruption and anti-bribery policies)
- Whistleblower/speak-up mechanisms
- Political engagement and lobbying activities
- Protection of whistleblowers

**Impact, Risk and Opportunity Management**
- Processes for preventing and detecting corruption and bribery
- Management of relationships with suppliers and payment terms

**Metrics and Targets**
- Confirmed incidents of corruption or bribery
- Legal actions related to anti-competitive behaviour
- Payment practices: average payment period to suppliers, proportion of payments made beyond agreed terms (particularly relevant for SME suppliers)
- Fines and settlements for ethical violations

---

## 3. Non-Material Topics — What You Still Need to Do

Even though Pollution (E2), Water (E3), Biodiversity (E4), Circular Economy (E5), Value Chain Workers (S2), Communities (S3), and Consumers/End-users (S4) are non-material, CSRD/ESRS imposes the following obligations:

1. **Document your assessment**: ESRS 2 requires you to describe the process and outcome of your double materiality assessment, including the rationale for exclusions.

2. **Disclose that these topics were assessed and found non-material**: Your sustainability statement should include a clear statement noting which ESRS topics were assessed and why they did not meet the materiality threshold.

3. **Revisit periodically**: Materiality is not static. You should reassess each reporting period. Changes in business model, supply chains, or operating context could make currently non-material topics material in the future.

4. **Sector-specific standards**: If sector-specific ESRS are finalized and applicable to your sector, they may require certain disclosures regardless of your materiality outcome — monitor EFRAG's work on sector standards.

5. **Phased-in requirements**: Some E1 and S1 metrics have transitional provisions allowing phase-in over the first 1–3 years of reporting. Check ESRS Appendix C for the specific list of phase-in reliefs.

---

## 4. Summary Table

| Standard | Applicability | Key Obligation |
|---|---|---|
| ESRS 1 | Always | Governs how you report — no disclosure requirements per se |
| ESRS 2 | Always mandatory | Full general disclosures including governance, strategy, materiality process |
| ESRS E1 | Material — full disclosure required | GHG emissions, transition plan, climate risks, energy use, targets |
| ESRS E2 (Pollution) | Non-material — no topical disclosures | Document why non-material |
| ESRS E3 (Water) | Non-material — no topical disclosures | Document why non-material |
| ESRS E4 (Biodiversity) | Non-material — no topical disclosures | Document why non-material |
| ESRS E5 (Circular Economy) | Non-material — no topical disclosures | Document why non-material |
| ESRS S1 | Material — full disclosure required | Workforce data, H&S, pay gap, diversity, training, remediation |
| ESRS S2 (Value Chain Workers) | Non-material — no topical disclosures | Document why non-material |
| ESRS S3 (Communities) | Non-material — no topical disclosures | Document why non-material |
| ESRS S4 (Consumers) | Non-material — no topical disclosures | Document why non-material |
| ESRS G1 | Material — full disclosure required | Anti-corruption, whistleblowing, payment practices, lobbying |

---

## 5. Practical Considerations

- **Connectivity to financial statements**: ESRS requires disclosures to be connected to your financial reporting where sustainability risks and impacts have financial implications. This is particularly relevant for E1 climate risks.

- **Value chain**: Even though S2–S4 are non-material, ESRS E1 and S1 may still require some consideration of your upstream supply chain (particularly for Scope 3 emissions under E1).

- **Assurance**: CSRD requires limited assurance of the sustainability statement (moving toward reasonable assurance over time). Your disclosures must be audit-ready.

- **Location**: The sustainability statement must be included in the management report (directors' report) as a dedicated section — it cannot be a standalone document.

- **Digital tagging**: Disclosures must be tagged using the European Single Electronic Format (ESEF) with the ESRS XBRL taxonomy once the taxonomy is finalized and applicable to your reporting period.

# GRI + TCFD to CSRD/ESRS Transition: Gap Assessment

## Executive Summary

If you already report under GRI Standards and publish a TCFD report, you have a meaningful head start — but you should expect **moderate-to-significant incremental work** to reach full CSRD/ESRS compliance. The good news: GRI and TCFD together cover a large portion of the climate and social disclosures required by ESRS. The challenge lies in CSRD's mandatory legal structure, its double materiality requirement, extensive governance disclosures, value chain obligations, digital tagging, and third-party assurance — none of which GRI or TCFD mandates.

A realistic estimate for a large company with mature GRI/TCFD reporting: **12–18 months of structured implementation work** before first reporting, assuming you run it in parallel with business-as-usual ESG reporting.

---

## What GRI and TCFD Give You (Your Starting Assets)

**From GRI Standards:**
- A materiality-assessed topic structure that maps broadly to ESRS topical standards (E1–E5, S1–S4, G1)
- Existing data collection processes for many quantitative disclosures (GHG, energy, water, waste, workforce metrics)
- Stakeholder engagement methodology
- Narrative disclosures on policies, targets, and management approaches

**From TCFD:**
- Climate-related governance disclosures (board and management roles) — directly useful for ESRS E1 and ESRS 2 GOV disclosures
- Climate risk scenario analysis (physical and transition risks) — maps to ESRS E1 physical and transition risk disclosures
- Metrics and targets for GHG emissions (Scope 1, 2, and likely Scope 3 at category level)
- Strategy disclosures on climate resilience

**GRI interoperability:** ESRS 1 Appendix C explicitly maps ESRS datapoints to GRI disclosures. GRI reporters can use this mapping to identify existing disclosures that already satisfy ESRS requirements, rather than starting from scratch.

**TCFD interoperability:** ESRS E1 incorporates TCFD recommendations directly. If your TCFD report covers governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics/targets for climate, you have the core architecture for ESRS E1.

---

## Gap Assessment Table

| ESRS Area | Current State (GRI + TCFD) | Gap | Priority | Recommended Action |
|-----------|---------------------------|-----|----------|--------------------|
| **ESRS 2 — Double Materiality Assessment (DMA)** | GRI uses impact materiality; TCFD uses financial materiality | GRI only covers one lens; no formal combined DMA process exists | **Critical** | Conduct a formal DMA integrating both impact and financial materiality per ESRS 1 paras. 45–56; document and disclose the process under SBM-3 |
| **ESRS 2 — Governance (GOV-1 to GOV-5)** | TCFD covers board/management climate roles; GRI covers some governance topics | GOV disclosures are broader than TCFD: must cover ALL sustainability topics, incentive schemes (GOV-3), internal controls for sustainability (GOV-5), and due diligence statement (GOV-4) | **High** | Map existing TCFD governance narrative to GOV-1/GOV-2; build out GOV-3 (incentives), GOV-4 (due diligence linkage), GOV-5 (risk controls) for all ESRS topics |
| **ESRS 2 — Strategy & Business Model (SBM-1, SBM-2, SBM-3)** | GRI partial; TCFD partial for climate | SBM-1 requires value chain description; SBM-2 requires documented stakeholder engagement per topic; SBM-3 requires full IRO disclosure tied to DMA | **High** | Expand strategy disclosures beyond climate; formalize stakeholder engagement documentation; link DMA outputs to SBM-3 |
| **ESRS E1 — Climate Change** | Strong: TCFD covers scenario analysis, governance, strategy, metrics/targets; GRI covers Scope 1/2/3 | Likely gaps: Scope 3 all 15 categories (if not already complete), GHG intensity per net revenue, EU Taxonomy alignment disclosures, transition plan with financial planning (capex/opex for decarbonisation), locked-in assets | **High** | Complete Scope 3 category inventory; prepare EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment calculation; draft ESRS-compliant transition plan per ESRS E1-1 |
| **ESRS E2 — Pollution** | GRI 305 (emissions) covers some; may have limited pollution disclosures | Likely a significant gap unless you are in a sector with heavy pollution relevance; specific ESRS E2 datapoints (substances of concern, pollution incidents, PRTR-linked disclosures) are more granular than typical GRI | **Medium** | Run DMA to determine materiality; if material, build data collection for air/water/soil pollutants and substances of concern |
| **ESRS E3 — Water & Marine Resources** | GRI 303 covers water withdrawal and consumption | GRI 303 aligns reasonably well; gap is likely in marine-specific disclosures and water stress area disaggregation | **Medium** | Cross-reference GRI 303 data to ESRS E3 datapoints; add water stress area breakdown if not already present |
| **ESRS E4 — Biodiversity & Ecosystems** | GRI 304 (biodiversity) is typically thin in most GRI reports | This is commonly the largest environmental gap for GRI reporters; ESRS E4 requires site-level biodiversity impact assessment, ecosystem services assessment, targets per the Kunming-Montreal framework | **High** | Assess biodiversity materiality in DMA; if material, engage specialist support for site-level assessment and ecosystem services mapping |
| **ESRS E5 — Resource Use & Circular Economy** | GRI 301 (materials), GRI 306 (waste) provide a base | ESRS E5 requires circular economy strategy disclosure and material flow data that goes beyond typical GRI waste disclosures | **Medium** | Map GRI 301/306 disclosures to ESRS E5 datapoints; identify gaps in circular economy strategy narrative |
| **ESRS S1 — Own Workforce** | GRI 400-series covers many workforce topics | Key gaps: gender pay gap disclosure (aligned with EU Pay Transparency Directive), collective bargaining coverage %, health & safety management system coverage, and more granular employee breakdown by country (for large companies) | **High** | Conduct ESRS S1 datapoint mapping against existing GRI 400-series data; build gender pay gap calculation and reporting process |
| **ESRS S2 — Workers in Value Chain** | GRI 408/409 cover some supply chain labour issues | ESRS S2 requires systematic value chain labour rights assessment — typically far more granular than GRI practice; data availability from suppliers is a common pain point | **High** | Map tier-1 supplier coverage; establish value chain data collection programme; use sector averages/proxies where direct data unavailable (disclose methodology) |
| **ESRS S3 — Affected Communities** | GRI 413 covers community impact | Typically a gap in formalised community IRO assessment and documentation tied to DMA | **Medium** | Assess materiality in DMA; if material, formalise community engagement and impact documentation |
| **ESRS S4 — Consumers & End-Users** | GRI 416/417/418 cover product safety and data | ESRS S4 requires consumer-related IRO process; may be covered adequately by GRI if disclosures are current | **Low–Medium** | Cross-reference existing GRI 416–418 disclosures to ESRS S4 datapoints |
| **ESRS G1 — Business Conduct** | GRI 205 (anti-corruption), GRI 206 (anti-competitive behaviour) provide a base | ESRS G1 adds payment practices (average payment days to suppliers), lobbying disclosure, and political contributions — often not in GRI reports | **Medium** | Add payment practices data collection; review lobbying and political contribution disclosures |
| **Reporting Location (Management Report)** | GRI report is typically standalone; TCFD may be in annual report | CSRD requires sustainability information in the management report (Accounting Directive Art. 19a), not as a standalone document | **High** | Work with legal/finance to integrate sustainability section into the annual management report; this requires coordination with auditors |
| **Digital Tagging (XBRL/iXBRL)** | Not applicable under GRI or TCFD | Full new requirement; all sustainability disclosures must be tagged using ESEF taxonomy (Commission sustainability taxonomy pending) | **High** | Engage reporting technology provider or work with finance team already using ESEF for financial statements; allow 3–6 months for taxonomy mapping and tagging setup |
| **Third-Party Assurance** | GRI assurance optional (many companies obtain it); TCFD no assurance requirement | CSRD requires limited assurance from statutory auditor or IASP from first reporting year (Art. 26a); this is a legal obligation, not optional | **Critical** | Engage statutory auditor or IASP now — assurance scope, readiness, and fees need to be agreed well before year-end; if you have GRI assurance, your provider may have a pathway |
| **Value Chain Data Collection** | GRI encourages but does not mandate systematic value chain data | CSRD requires value chain impacts, risks, and opportunities to be assessed where material; data from suppliers and downstream partners is needed | **High** | Run value chain mapping exercise tied to DMA; build supplier data requests into procurement contracts; begin with material topics only |

---

## Top Gaps to Prioritise

### 1. Double Materiality Assessment — Start Immediately
Your GRI materiality process covers only impact materiality. TCFD covers financial materiality for climate only. CSRD requires a combined DMA across all ESRS topics. This is the **foundation of your entire CSRD report** — without it, you cannot determine which topical standards apply or which datapoints to collect. Begin the DMA process at least 12 months before your first reporting year.

### 2. Assurance Readiness — Engage Your Auditor Now
Limited assurance is legally required from day one. Many statutory auditors are developing CSRD assurance methodologies. Engaging early allows you to understand what evidence they will require, which will drive your data governance and documentation approach. If you currently obtain GRI assurance, your existing provider may be well-positioned to extend scope.

### 3. Scope 3 Completeness and Value Chain Data
Most GRI reporters disclose Scope 3 selectively. ESRS E1 requires all 15 Scope 3 categories if climate is material, with clear disclosure of estimation methodology. Value chain social data (ESRS S2) is also a common and significant gap, requiring supplier engagement programmes.

### 4. Biodiversity (ESRS E4)
This is the most frequent "surprise" gap for GRI reporters. Unless you have already aligned with TNFD or published detailed biodiversity disclosures, expect to build this largely from scratch if it is material after your DMA.

### 5. Governance Integration and Incentives (ESRS 2 GOV)
TCFD governance disclosures cover climate. ESRS 2 GOV requires board and management oversight of all material sustainability topics, disclosure of sustainability-linked incentive schemes, and internal controls over sustainability reporting — significantly broader than most existing frameworks require.

### 6. Management Report Integration and XBRL Tagging
These are structural/legal requirements with no equivalent in GRI or TCFD. They require coordination across finance, legal, IT, and sustainability teams and typically take 6–12 months to implement properly.

---

## Realistic Work Estimate

| Phase | Timeline | Key Activities |
|-------|----------|---------------|
| **Scoping & DMA** | Months 1–4 | Confirm CSRD applicability, conduct DMA, identify material ESRS topics |
| **Gap Analysis** | Months 3–5 | Map existing GRI/TCFD disclosures to ESRS datapoints topic by topic |
| **Data Architecture** | Months 4–9 | Build data collection processes for gaps (value chain, pay gap, biodiversity, Scope 3 completeness) |
| **Governance & Policy** | Months 5–8 | Establish board oversight processes, sustainability governance documentation, due diligence statement |
| **Reporting Integration** | Months 7–11 | Draft ESRS disclosures, integrate into management report structure, prepare XBRL tagging |
| **Assurance Preparation** | Months 6–12 | Engage auditor, build evidence trail, conduct pre-assurance readiness review |
| **First CSRD Report Published** | End of Year 1 or 2 (depending on your scope category) | Full ESRS-compliant report with limited assurance |

---

## Key References

- **ESRS 1, Appendix C** — GRI-to-ESRS mapping (use this to identify which existing GRI disclosures satisfy ESRS datapoints)
- **ESRS 2, GOV-1 to GOV-5, SBM-1 to SBM-3, IRO-1** — mandatory for all in-scope companies regardless of DMA
- **ESRS E1** — incorporates TCFD recommendations; TCFD reporters have a strong foundation but gaps exist on EU Taxonomy, transition plan financial detail, and Scope 3 completeness
- **Art. 19a CSRD (Directive 2022/2464)** — management report location requirement
- **Art. 26a CSRD** — assurance obligation
- **Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772** — ESRS standards text

**Note on the Omnibus Proposal (February 2025):** The European Commission has proposed simplifications that may narrow the scope of CSRD and reduce mandatory datapoints, particularly for the second wave of reporters. Monitor the legislative status of this proposal, as it may affect which ESRS topical standards are mandatory versus voluntary for your reporting category. However, the core DMA, ESRS 2 general disclosures, assurance, and management report location requirements are unlikely to be removed.

# Transitioning from GRI Standards and TCFD to CSRD/ESRS: Gap Analysis and Effort Assessment

## Executive Summary

If your organization already reports under GRI Standards and TCFD, you have a meaningful head start on CSRD/ESRS compliance. However, transitioning is not a simple mapping exercise. CSRD/ESRS introduces a more prescriptive, auditable, and legally binding framework with significant new requirements that neither GRI nor TCFD fully address. Expect a moderate-to-substantial effort depending on your organization's size, sector, and current reporting maturity.

---

## What You Already Have: Your Starting Advantages

### From GRI Standards
GRI provides a strong foundation for the social and governance dimensions of ESRS. Key areas of alignment include:

- **Stakeholder engagement processes** — GRI's materiality approach involves stakeholder dialogue, which partially supports ESRS's double materiality requirements.
- **Social disclosures** — GRI 400-series (Labor, Human Rights, Society) maps reasonably well to ESRS S1 (Own Workforce), S2 (Workers in the Value Chain), S3 (Affected Communities), and S4 (Consumers and End-users).
- **Governance disclosures** — GRI 2 (General Disclosures) overlaps with ESRS G1 (Business Conduct) and ESRS 2 governance disclosures.
- **Environmental topic coverage** — GRI 300-series (Energy, Water, Emissions, Waste, Biodiversity) provides baseline data that feeds into ESRS E1–E5.
- **Reporting infrastructure** — Existing data collection systems, internal controls, and reporting workflows can be adapted rather than built from scratch.

### From TCFD
TCFD was the primary precursor to ESRS E1 (Climate Change) and provides strong alignment for:

- **Climate governance** — Board and management oversight of climate risk maps directly to ESRS 2 GOV disclosures.
- **Risk and opportunity identification** — TCFD's risk/opportunity framework aligns with ESRS E1's physical and transition risk disclosures.
- **Scenario analysis** — If you have conducted TCFD scenario analysis, this work is directly reusable for ESRS E1 requirements on climate scenario analysis.
- **Metrics and targets** — Scope 1, 2, and 3 GHG emissions, and climate-related financial metrics, are required in both frameworks.

---

## Key Gaps: Where Significant Work Is Still Required

### 1. Double Materiality Assessment (Critical Gap)
**Effort: High**

This is the single most significant structural gap. ESRS requires a rigorous **double materiality assessment** that evaluates:
- **Impact materiality**: How does your company affect people and the environment (positive and negative, actual and potential, across the value chain)?
- **Financial materiality**: How do sustainability matters affect your company's financial position and performance?

GRI uses a single-axis stakeholder-informed materiality process. TCFD uses financial materiality only. ESRS requires both simultaneously and with documented, auditable methodology. This assessment determines which ESRS topic standards apply to you and must be defensible to auditors. Most organizations undergoing CSRD transition find this to be their most time-consuming workload.

### 2. Value Chain Disclosures (Significant Gap)
**Effort: High**

ESRS extends disclosure requirements far into the upstream and downstream value chain — suppliers, contractors, distribution partners, and end customers. GRI encourages but does not mandate this depth. TCFD is primarily focused on the reporting entity itself. You will likely need:
- Supplier data collection programs or surveys
- Contractual requirements with key suppliers
- Estimation methodologies where direct data is unavailable
- Governance frameworks for value chain oversight

### 3. Biodiversity and Ecosystems — ESRS E4 (Significant Gap)
**Effort: Medium to High**

Unless you have voluntarily adopted TNFD or similar frameworks, biodiversity is likely a major gap. ESRS E4 requires:
- Site-specific assessments of biodiversity-sensitive locations
- Metrics on land use, species impact, and ecosystem degradation
- Alignment with EU Biodiversity Strategy targets

GRI 304 (Biodiversity) exists but is rarely reported with the granularity ESRS E4 demands. TCFD does not address biodiversity.

### 4. Resource Use and Circular Economy — ESRS E5 (Moderate Gap)
**Effort: Medium**

ESRS E5 on resource use and circular economy goes beyond what GRI 301 (Materials) and GRI 306 (Waste) typically cover, requiring:
- Inflows and outflows of resources tracked against circular economy principles
- Products and materials designed for reuse, repair, and recyclability
- Alignment with EU Circular Economy Action Plan targets

### 5. Own Workforce Detail — ESRS S1 (Moderate Gap)
**Effort: Medium**

ESRS S1 is substantially more granular than most GRI reporters achieve in practice. New requirements include:
- Detailed breakdown of workforce by employment type, contract type, gender, age, and region
- Living wage assessments and coverage rates
- More specific health and safety metrics
- Collective bargaining and freedom of association data at a greater level of specificity
- Disclosures on non-employee workers (contractors, agency workers)

### 6. Narrative and Policy Disclosures (Moderate Gap)
**Effort: Medium**

Each ESRS topic standard requires a structured set of disclosures covering:
- **Policies** in place addressing the topic
- **Actions and resources** allocated
- **Targets** set and progress against them
- **Metrics** (both mandatory and entity-specific)

GRI reporters often have partial versions of these, but ESRS requires them to follow a specific, mandatory structure. Retrofitting existing narrative disclosures to this architecture takes significant editorial and governance effort.

### 7. Assurance Readiness (Significant Gap for Most)
**Effort: Medium to High**

CSRD mandates **limited assurance** from the outset, with a trajectory toward **reasonable assurance**. This requires:
- Internal controls over sustainability reporting comparable to financial reporting controls
- Audit trails and data documentation
- Cross-functional governance (sustainability, finance, legal, operations)
- Engagement with external auditors who will scrutinize not just disclosures but data processes

Most GRI and TCFD reporters have not built sustainability data infrastructure to this standard. This is often the area that requires the most investment in systems and process redesign.

### 8. ESRS 2 — General Disclosures (Moderate Gap)
**Effort: Medium**

ESRS 2 is mandatory for all in-scope entities regardless of double materiality outcomes. It requires structured disclosures on:
- Governance bodies and their sustainability roles
- Management of sustainability-related impacts, risks, and opportunities
- Strategy and business model integration
- Stakeholder engagement processes (more detailed than GRI's approach)
- The double materiality assessment methodology itself

While GRI 2 and TCFD governance disclosures cover some of this ground, ESRS 2 has a more prescriptive format that will require dedicated structuring work.

## Key Recommendations

1. **Start with the double materiality assessment.** Everything else in ESRS is conditioned on its outputs. Invest in a rigorous, documented methodology early.

2. **Do a structured GRI-to-ESRS mapping exercise.** Many GRI disclosures have direct or partial equivalents in ESRS. Identify what you can reuse and what needs enhancement versus what must be built from scratch.

3. **Treat TCFD as your ESRS E1 foundation.** Your climate scenario analysis, risk identification, and metrics work is directly transferable — focus on filling gaps (e.g., physical risk at asset level, Scope 3 completeness, transition plan requirements under ESRS E1).

4. **Prioritize value chain data collection.** This typically has the longest lead time and requires external partner engagement. Start scoping supplier data programs early.

5. **Engage your assurance provider early.** Understanding what your auditors will expect shapes how you build data processes. Early engagement prevents costly rework.

6. **Assess ESRS E4 (Biodiversity) carefully.** If your double materiality assessment flags biodiversity as material, this is likely your largest net-new disclosure workload.

7. **Invest in data infrastructure.** CSRD-grade reporting requires sustainability data to be managed with the same rigor as financial data. This often means upgrading ESG data management systems.

# CSRD Scope Analysis: Non-EU Company with EU Subsidiaries

## Your Situation at a Glance

**Yes, CSRD applies to your group.** As a US-headquartered technology company with €200M in EU net turnover and qualifying EU subsidiaries, you fall within the CSRD's third-country undertaking provisions. Your first mandatory reporting year is **FY 2028**, with the report published in **2029**.

---

## Scope / Threshold Analysis

### Step 1: Non-EU Company Threshold Test (Art. 40a CSRD)

CSRD Art. 40a (transposed from Directive 2013/34/EU as amended) extends the directive's reach to non-EU parent undertakings that generate significant EU revenue and have qualifying EU-based entities.

| Criterion | Threshold | Your Position | Met? |
|-----------|-----------|---------------|------|
| Net turnover generated in the EU | > €150M | €200M combined from German and French subsidiaries | **YES** |
| Qualifying EU subsidiary (large company OR listed) | ≥ 1 large EU subsidiary or branch with >€40M EU turnover | German subsidiary: 600 employees (see Step 2) | **YES** |

**Verdict: Both criteria are satisfied. CSRD applies to your group.**

### Step 2: German Subsidiary — Large Company Test (Art. 3(4) Directive 2013/34/EU)

A company qualifies as "large" under EU law if it exceeds **at least 2 of the following 3 thresholds**:

| Size Criterion | Threshold | German Subsidiary |
|----------------|-----------|-------------------|
| Number of employees | > 250 | **600** — Exceeds |
| Net turnover | > €40M | Not stated, but likely exceeded given total EU revenue of €200M |
| Total assets | > €20M | Not stated |

With 600 employees, the German subsidiary already exceeds one threshold definitively. Given it is part of a group generating €200M in EU revenue, it almost certainly also exceeds the €40M turnover threshold. If so, it qualifies as a **large EU subsidiary**, satisfying the second prong of the Art. 40a test.

**If the German subsidiary's standalone turnover exceeds €40M (highly probable given group revenues), it qualifies as a large company even without being listed.**

The French subsidiary further reinforces the group's EU footprint.

### Step 3: First Reporting Year

| Category | First Reporting Year | Report Published |
|----------|---------------------|-----------------|
| Non-EU companies (Art. 40a) | **FY 2028** | **2029** |

---

## What CSRD Requires from You

### Who Files the Report?

Under Art. 40a, the **EU subsidiaries themselves** (specifically, the large ones — here, the German subsidiary and potentially the French subsidiary) are obligated to publish a CSRD-compliant sustainability report. There is no option for the US parent to file a consolidated ESRS report at parent level as a substitute — the obligation sits at the EU subsidiary level unless an equivalent third-country parent report is accepted (see "Group Reporting" below).

**Practical implication:** Your German subsidiary is the primary obligated entity. If the French subsidiary also qualifies as large, it bears its own obligation.

### Reporting Standard

Non-EU company subsidiaries report under the **ESRS standards** (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772) — the same standards as EU large companies. There is a sector-agnostic set of ESRS for non-EU undertakings currently being developed by EFRAG (the "ESRS for third-country undertakings"), though EU subsidiaries of non-EU groups will use the standard ESRS unless a specific equivalence decision has been made.

---

## Key Obligations — What You Need to Do

### 1. Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) — The Starting Point

Before any disclosure can be prepared, the German (and French) subsidiary must conduct a **Double Materiality Assessment** (ESRS 1, paras. 45–56). This determines which ESRS topical standards apply.

**Two lenses:**
- **Impact materiality:** Does the subsidiary's technology operations cause actual or potential impacts on people or the environment (e.g., digital waste, energy use in data centres, workforce conditions)?
- **Financial materiality:** Do sustainability factors create risks or opportunities for the subsidiary's financial performance (e.g., physical climate risk to EU offices, regulatory cost from carbon pricing)?

A topic is material if it meets **either** lens. As a technology company, the DMA will likely identify climate (energy, GHG from data centres), workforce (ESRS S1), and business conduct (ESRS G1) as highly probable material topics.

### 2. Mandatory Disclosures — ESRS 2 (All In-Scope Companies)

Regardless of DMA outcomes, **ESRS 2 General Disclosures are mandatory** for all in-scope entities. These cover:

| Disclosure | Content Required |
|------------|-----------------|
| **GOV-1** | Role of board/supervisory bodies in sustainability oversight |
| **GOV-2** | Management's role and sustainability expertise |
| **GOV-3** | Sustainability-linked incentive schemes |
| **GOV-4** | Due diligence statement (alignment with UN Guiding Principles, OECD Guidelines) |
| **GOV-5** | Risk management and internal controls for sustainability |
| **SBM-1** | Business model, strategy, and value chain description |
| **SBM-2** | Interests and views of stakeholders |
| **SBM-3** | Material impacts, risks, and opportunities (output of DMA) |
| **IRO-1** | Process for identifying and assessing material IROs |

### 3. Likely Material Topical Standards for a Technology Company

| ESRS Standard | Topic | Likely Applicability |
|---------------|-------|---------------------|
| **ESRS E1** | Climate Change | High — data centres, office energy consumption, business travel, Scope 3 supply chain emissions |
| **ESRS S1** | Own Workforce | High — 600+ employees in Germany alone; pay gap, collective bargaining, H&S, training |
| **ESRS G1** | Business Conduct | High — anti-corruption, data ethics, supplier practices |
| **ESRS E5** | Resource Use & Circular Economy | Medium — hardware lifecycle, e-waste |
| **ESRS S4** | Consumers & End-Users | Medium — data privacy, product safety obligations |
| **ESRS S2** | Workers in Value Chain | Medium — supply chain labour practices |

Note: The DMA will determine the definitive list.

### 4. Key Datapoints to Prepare (Illustrative for E1 and S1)

**ESRS E1 — Climate (if material):**
- Scope 1 GHG emissions (direct, e.g., fleet, on-site combustion)
- Scope 2 GHG emissions (electricity — both market-based and location-based)
- Scope 3 GHG emissions across all 15 categories (especially Categories 1, 3, 6, 11 for tech companies)
- Energy consumption and renewable energy share
- GHG reduction targets (Paris-aligned, 2030/2050)
- Climate transition plan (Art. 19a(2)(a))
- EU Taxonomy eligible and aligned revenue/capex/opex

**ESRS S1 — Own Workforce (if material):**
- Total headcount by gender, contract type, country
- Gender pay gap (aligned with EU Pay Transparency Directive)
- % employees covered by collective bargaining agreements
- Work-related injury rate (LTIFR) and fatalities
- Training hours per employee
- Employee turnover rate

### 5. Value Chain Reporting

CSRD requires consideration of the **upstream and downstream value chain** where material (ESRS 1). As a technology company, this means:

- **Upstream:** Hardware suppliers, cloud infrastructure partners, component manufacturers
- **Downstream:** Customer use-phase emissions (Scope 3 Category 11), end-of-life product disposal

Where supplier data is unavailable, proxy data and sector averages may be used, but the methodology and limitations must be disclosed.

### 6. Group Reporting — Can the US Parent File on Behalf of Subsidiaries?

Under Art. 19a(9) and related provisions, a subsidiary may be **exempt from its own CSRD filing** if:
- It is included in a **consolidated sustainability report** prepared by a parent undertaking, AND
- That parent's report complies with CSRD or an **equivalent standard** as determined by the European Commission

Currently, **no third-country standard has been formally declared equivalent** by the Commission. This means:
- A US parent reporting under GRI, TCFD, or SEC climate disclosure rules alone **cannot substitute** for CSRD compliance at the EU subsidiary level
- However, if the Commission declares equivalence for a US framework in the future, this option may become available

**Practical path:** The German subsidiary (and French subsidiary if large) must file their own ESRS-compliant reports unless and until equivalence is formally granted.

### 7. Report Format and Assurance Requirements

| Requirement | Details |
|-------------|---------|
| **Location** | Dedicated section of the German subsidiary's management report (Lagesbericht) — not a standalone sustainability document |
| **Digital tagging** | XBRL/iXBRL tagging required (ESEF format) per Art. 19a CSRD |
| **Third-party assurance** | **Limited assurance** required from first reporting year (Art. 26a) — by a statutory auditor (Wirtschaftsprüfer in Germany) or accredited IASP |
| **Reasonable assurance** | Phased in later (Commission review by 2028) |

## Critical Considerations and Risks

### 1. French Subsidiary Threshold Confirmation
The question does not specify the French subsidiary's employee count or standalone turnover. If the French subsidiary also qualifies as a large company (≥2 of: >250 employees, >€40M turnover, >€20M assets), it bears **its own independent CSRD obligation**. ### 2. German Subsidiary Standalone Turnover
Confirm that the German subsidiary's standalone turnover exceeds €40M. While highly probable given the group's €200M EU revenue, this should be formally verified to ensure the Art. 40a trigger is met.

### 3. CSRD Omnibus Package (2025)
The European Commission proposed a simplification package in February 2025 (the "CSRD Omnibus") that may:
- Narrow the scope of companies subject to CSRD
- Reduce the number of mandatory datapoints
- Potentially raise thresholds

As of the current date (May 2026), monitor the legislative status of the Omnibus Package. The FY 2028 timeline and current ESRS obligations remain the baseline until formal changes are enacted.

### 4. German Codetermination and Works Council
The German subsidiary's 600 employees will trigger German codetermination rules (Mitbestimmungsgesetz). Any CSRD-related data collection on workforce matters (ESRS S1) should be coordinated with the **Betriebsrat (works council)**, as workforce data collection may require consultation or agreement under German labour law.

### 5. Intragroup Data Sharing
The US parent will need to consider **data governance arrangements** for sharing sustainability data between the parent and EU subsidiaries. This intersects with GDPR obligations for any personal data elements (e.g., headcount by gender, pay gap data). Ensure data transfer mechanisms are in place.

# CSRD Applicability for a US-Headquartered Company with EU Subsidiaries

## Summary Answer

Yes, CSRD likely applies to your situation — but the obligations fall on your EU subsidiaries, not directly on the US parent company. Based on the facts provided, your German subsidiary almost certainly qualifies as a large undertaking under CSRD and will be required to publish a sustainability report. There is also a potential obligation at the consolidated (group) level if the EU group as a whole meets the thresholds.

---

## 1. CSRD Background and Scope

The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), adopted in December 2022 and effective from January 2023, significantly expands the EU's non-financial reporting requirements. It replaces the Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD) and is implemented into national law by EU member states (Germany and France have both transposed it).

CSRD applies to:
- Large EU companies (including subsidiaries of non-EU groups)
- Non-EU parent companies with significant EU activity (via a separate "third-country undertaking" rule)
- EU-listed SMEs (with a later opt-out period)

---

## 2. Does CSRD Apply to You as a Non-EU Company?

### Direct Obligation on the US Parent (Third-Country Undertaking Rule)

Under Article 40 of CSRD (the "third-country undertaking" provision), a non-EU parent company is directly subject to CSRD reporting if it meets **both** of the following thresholds:

- **Net turnover in the EU exceeds €150 million** for each of the last two consecutive financial years, AND
- The company has either:
  - At least one EU subsidiary that is a large undertaking or a listed SME, OR
  - At least one EU branch generating more than €40 million net turnover

**Your situation:** With €200M in combined EU revenue, you exceed the €150M EU turnover threshold. You also have at least one EU subsidiary (the German subsidiary with 600 employees), which, as shown below, qualifies as a large undertaking.

**Conclusion:** The US parent company is subject to the third-country undertaking rule and must publish a group-level sustainability report covering EU operations. This report must be filed by a designated EU subsidiary (typically the largest one, in your case likely the German subsidiary) and must comply with the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) or an equivalent standard recognized by the European Commission.

**Timing for third-country undertakings:** The obligation for non-EU parent companies applies for financial years starting on or after **1 January 2028** (with first reports due in 2029), under the current CSRD timeline. Note that the EU has proposed and in some cases adopted deferrals — you should confirm the current timeline as it may have been adjusted.

---

### Obligation on the German Subsidiary (Large Undertaking Rule)

Independently of the parent company's obligations, each EU subsidiary must be assessed against the CSRD thresholds for large undertakings. A company qualifies as a "large undertaking" under EU Accounting Directive criteria if it exceeds **at least two of the three** following thresholds:

| Criterion | Threshold |
|---|---|
| Balance sheet total | > €25 million |
| Net turnover | > €50 million |
| Average number of employees | > 250 |

**Your German subsidiary:**
- Employees: 600 (exceeds the 250 threshold)
- Revenue: The combined EU revenue is €200M across Germany and France. Even if split, it is highly likely the German subsidiary alone exceeds €50M net turnover given the scale of operations.
- Balance sheet: Not stated, but a technology company with 600 employees and >€50M revenue would typically exceed €25M in balance sheet total.

**Conclusion:** The German subsidiary almost certainly meets two or more thresholds and qualifies as a large undertaking under CSRD. It is therefore independently required to report under CSRD.

**Timing for large undertakings:** For companies that were not previously subject to NFRD (non-public-interest entities), the obligation applies for financial years starting on or after **1 January 2025** (with first reports due in 2026). However, given recent EU "Omnibus" simplification proposals in early 2025, this timeline may have been deferred — confirm the current applicable dates.

**French subsidiary:** Similarly, the French subsidiary should be assessed against the same thresholds independently.

---

## 3. What Do You Need to Do?

### Step 1: Confirm Subsidiary-Level Thresholds

- Obtain the precise revenue, balance sheet, and headcount figures for both the German and French subsidiaries separately.
- Determine whether each subsidiary independently meets at least two of the three large undertaking thresholds.
- If both subsidiaries qualify, each may need its own CSRD-compliant sustainability report (unless a consolidated report at the EU sub-group level is permitted and elected).

### Step 2: Assess the Third-Country Undertaking Obligation

- Confirm that combined EU net turnover has exceeded €150M for each of the past two consecutive financial years.
- Identify which EU subsidiary will be designated to file the group sustainability report on behalf of the US parent.
- Track the third-country undertaking reporting timeline (currently financial years from 1 January 2028).

### Step 3: Determine Reporting Structure

You have two main structural options:

**Option A — Subsidiary-Level Reports Only**
Each qualifying subsidiary reports individually. This is simpler but may result in duplicative effort and does not satisfy the third-country undertaking obligation at the parent level.

**Option B — Consolidated EU Sub-Group Report**
A designated EU subsidiary (e.g., the German subsidiary) publishes a consolidated sustainability report covering all EU subsidiaries. This can satisfy both the large undertaking obligation and (from 2028) the third-country undertaking obligation, provided the report meets the required standards.

### Step 4: Align with European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS)

CSRD reports must follow the ESRS, developed by EFRAG (European Financial Reporting Advisory Group). Key ESRS requirements include:

- **Double materiality assessment:** Identify sustainability topics that are material both from a financial perspective (how ESG issues affect the company) and an impact perspective (how the company affects people and the environment).
- **Mandatory disclosures:** Certain general disclosures (ESRS 2) are mandatory for all reporting entities.
- **Topical standards:** Additional disclosures on climate (ESRS E1), pollution, biodiversity, water, workers, affected communities, business conduct, and governance — required based on materiality assessment outcomes.
- **Value chain disclosures:** You must report on sustainability matters across your upstream and downstream value chain where material.

### Step 5: Third-Party Assurance

CSRD requires **limited assurance** on sustainability reports from an independent auditor, with a pathway to reasonable assurance in future years. Engage your statutory auditor or an accredited third-party assurance provider early.

### Step 6: Integration with Annual Report

CSRD requires the sustainability report to be published as a dedicated section of the management report (annual report) — it cannot be a standalone document separate from the financial reporting package.

### Step 7: XBRL Tagging

Sustainability disclosures must be tagged in XBRL (iXBRL) format using the ESRS taxonomy to enable machine-readable reporting and submission via the European Single Electronic Format (ESEF).

### Step 8: Governance and Data Infrastructure

- Appoint a CSRD project owner at the subsidiary level (and group level for the parent).
- Map data collection responsibilities across business units: HR, operations, procurement, finance, legal.
- Implement a sustainability data management system capable of collecting and auditing ESG metrics.
- Update board-level governance to include oversight of sustainability reporting.

---

## 4. Key Deadlines (as of Knowledge Cutoff — Verify for Updates)

| Entity Type | Reporting for FY | First Report Due |
|---|---|---|
| Large EU undertakings (non-NFRD) | FY 2025 | 2026 |
| Third-country undertakings (non-EU parents) | FY 2028 | 2029 |

**Important caveat:** The European Commission launched an "Omnibus" simplification package in early 2025 that proposed deferring CSRD obligations for certain companies by two years and narrowing scope. As of mid-2025, legislative negotiations were ongoing. You must verify the current applicable timeline with EU legal counsel or by checking the latest Official Journal of the EU.

---

## 5. Practical Recommendations

1. **Engage EU legal counsel** in Germany and France immediately to confirm national transposition specifics and any local regulatory guidance.
2. **Conduct a double materiality assessment** as the foundation for all ESRS disclosures — this is time-consuming and should begin 12–18 months before the first report is due.
3. **Assess whether the ESRS or an equivalent standard** (e.g., GRI, if recognized by the Commission) will be used for the third-country undertaking report.
4. **Coordinate reporting across subsidiaries** to avoid inconsistent disclosures and reduce duplication.
5. **Engage your auditor early** on assurance scope, methodology, and readiness requirements.
6. **Monitor legislative developments** — the Omnibus package may materially change your obligations and timelines.

---

## Conclusion

CSRD applies to your organization in two ways: (1) your German subsidiary is independently required to report as a large EU undertaking, and likely your French subsidiary as well; and (2) the US parent company is subject to the third-country undertaking rule given €200M in EU revenue and the presence of large EU subsidiaries. The immediate compliance priority is preparing the German (and potentially French) subsidiary for their large undertaking reporting obligations. Planning for the parent-level consolidated report should begin now given the complexity of ESRS implementation.

# CIS Controls v8: Implementation Group Scoping for a 75-Person Accounting Firm

---

## 1. Organization Profile

| Attribute | Your Organization |
|-----------|------------------|
| **Size** | 75 employees |
| **Industry** | Accounting / Professional Services |
| **IT Staffing** | 1 part-time IT generalist |
| **Data Sensitivity** | High — client financial and tax data (PII, financial records) |
| **Technology Stack** | Cloud-based accounting software, Microsoft 365 |
| **Prior Security Assessments** | None |
| **Regulatory Exposure** | IRS Safeguards Program (if handling tax data), state CPA board requirements, potentially FTC Safeguards Rule |

---

## 2. Implementation Group Determination

### Recommended IG: **IG2 (with immediate IG1 foundation)**

**Rationale:**

You sit at the upper boundary of IG1 and clearly cross into **IG2** based on the following criteria:

| IG Criterion | Your Situation |
|---|---|
| **Data sensitivity** | You process client financial and tax data — this is highly sensitive data that, if compromised, would materially harm your clients and expose your firm to liability. This is the defining IG2 signal. |
| **IT capability** | One part-time IT person is limited, but you do have *someone responsible for managing and protecting IT* — the IG2 criterion is met. IG1 is specifically for organizations with *no dedicated IT function*. |
| **Operational impact** | A breach or extended outage would significantly impact client service delivery and could trigger regulatory reporting obligations. You can withstand *some* outage, but not prolonged disruption. |
| **Commercial off-the-shelf tools** | Your stack (Microsoft 365, cloud accounting software) is commercially supported — consistent with both IG1 and IG2. |
| **Regulatory oversight** | Tax data handling brings IRS and FTC Safeguards Rule exposure. If you have more than 5,000 customer records, the FTC Safeguards Rule (16 CFR Part 314) mandates a formal written information security program — directly driving IG2 controls. |

**You are not IG3** because you do not employ dedicated security experts, you are not subject to rigorous regulatory audits (e.g., HIPAA, PCI, FEDRAMP), and a breach — while serious — would not cause "significant harm to public welfare."

**Practical guidance:** Since you have never done a formal security assessment, **begin by achieving full IG1 compliance first**, then systematically layer in IG2 safeguards. Trying to implement all 130 IG2 safeguards simultaneously will overwhelm a part-time IT resource.

---

## 3. IG1 Foundation: Where to Start (56 Safeguards Across 18 Controls)

The following is a prioritized starting sequence tailored to your environment. Work through these in order — each builds on the last.

---

### Phase 1: Know What You Have (Weeks 1–4)

**CIS Control 1 — Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets**
- **Safeguard 1.1:** Create and maintain a detailed inventory of all devices: laptops, desktops, phones, printers, routers. Use a spreadsheet or Microsoft Intune (already available in M365) to track device name, owner, OS version, and location.
- **Safeguard 1.2:** Identify and address any unauthorized devices found on the network.
- **Why first:** You cannot protect what you do not know exists. This is the prerequisite for every other control.

**CIS Control 2 — Inventory and Control of Software Assets**
- **Safeguard 2.1:** Document all software authorized to run on firm devices, including your cloud accounting platform, M365 apps, and any installed applications.
- **Safeguard 2.2:** Confirm all software is currently vendor-supported (no end-of-life OS or applications).
- **Safeguard 2.3:** Remove or disable unauthorized software.

**CIS Control 3 — Data Protection (IG1 Safeguards)**
- **Safeguard 3.1:** Establish a data management process — define what client data you hold, where it lives, and who can access it.
- **Safeguard 3.2:** Maintain a data inventory (e.g., "client tax returns stored in [cloud platform]; client PII in M365 SharePoint").
- **Safeguard 3.3:** Configure access control lists — client data should be accessible only to staff working on that client.
- **Safeguard 3.4/3.5:** Define data retention periods and a secure disposal process for old records (shredding, secure deletion).

---

### Phase 2: Protect Accounts and Access (Weeks 3–6)

**CIS Control 5 — Account Management**
- **Safeguard 5.1:** Inventory all user accounts in Microsoft 365 and your accounting software. Remove former employee accounts immediately.
- **Safeguard 5.2:** Enforce unique, strong passwords. Use Microsoft 365's password policies and ban common passwords.
- **Safeguard 5.3:** Disable or remove accounts for departed employees and inactive accounts (no activity in 90 days).
- **Safeguard 5.4:** Restrict admin privileges — only the IT person (and a designated backup) should have global admin in M365. Partners should not use admin accounts for daily work.

**CIS Control 6 — Access Control Management (IG1 Safeguards)**
- **Safeguard 6.1:** Establish a formal process for granting access (new hire checklist).
- **Safeguard 6.2:** Establish a formal process for revoking access (offboarding checklist — same day as termination).

> **Critical note for your firm:** Multi-factor authentication (MFA) for externally-exposed applications (Safeguard 6.3) is technically an IG2 safeguard, but given that you process client financial data through cloud applications accessible over the internet, **treat this as an immediate priority regardless of IG level**. Enable MFA for all Microsoft 365 accounts and your cloud accounting platform now. This single action prevents the majority of credential-based attacks.

---

### Phase 3: Harden Systems and Prevent Malware (Weeks 5–8)

**CIS Control 4 — Secure Configuration**
- **Safeguard 4.1:** Document baseline security configurations for all devices. Use Microsoft Security Baseline templates (free from Microsoft).
- **Safeguard 4.3:** Configure automatic screen lock after 15 minutes of inactivity on all devices.
- **Safeguard 4.4/4.5:** Enable host-based firewalls on all servers and end-user devices. Windows Defender Firewall is already available.

**CIS Control 10 — Malware Defenses**
- **Safeguard 10.1:** Deploy anti-malware on all endpoints. Microsoft Defender (included in M365 Business Premium) covers this.
- **Safeguard 10.2:** Confirm automatic signature updates are enabled.
- **Safeguard 10.3:** Disable AutoRun/AutoPlay on all Windows devices.
- **Safeguard 10.4:** Configure anti-malware scanning of removable media (USB drives).

---

### Phase 4: Patching and Backups (Weeks 7–10)

**CIS Control 7 — Continuous Vulnerability Management (IG1 Safeguards)**
- **Safeguard 7.1:** Create a vulnerability management process — at minimum, a monthly patching schedule.
- **Safeguard 7.2:** Document a remediation process: critical patches within 14 days, high within 30 days.
- **Safeguard 7.3:** Enable automatic OS patch management for all Windows/Mac devices. Microsoft Intune or Windows Update for Business (included in M365) handles this.
- **Safeguard 7.4:** Enable automatic application patch management. Enable auto-updates for all third-party apps.

**CIS Control 11 — Data Recovery**
- **Safeguard 11.1:** Document your backup and recovery process.
- **Safeguard 11.2:** Implement automated backups of all critical data. Your cloud accounting platform likely has built-in backups — verify this. For M365, enable Microsoft 365 Backup or use a third-party backup (Veeam, Acronis).
- **Safeguard 11.4:** Maintain an isolated backup copy (offline or separate cloud tenant) to protect against ransomware. This is non-negotiable for a firm handling financial data.

---

### Phase 5: Email, Web, and Logging (Weeks 9–12)

**CIS Control 9 — Email and Web Browser Protections**
- **Safeguard 9.1:** Ensure all browsers and email clients are fully supported and up-to-date.
- **Safeguard 9.2:** Enable DNS filtering (Microsoft Defender for Endpoint includes this; Cisco Umbrella or Cloudflare Gateway are low-cost alternatives).
- **Safeguard 9.3:** Configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC DNS records for your email domain to prevent spoofing. This is free and critical for an accounting firm targeted by business email compromise (BEC) attacks.

**CIS Control 8 — Audit Log Management (IG1 Safeguards)**
- **Safeguard 8.1:** Define a log management process.
- **Safeguard 8.2:** Enable audit logging in Microsoft 365 (Microsoft Purview Audit). Confirm logging is enabled in your cloud accounting platform.

---

### Phase 6: Training and Incident Response (Ongoing)

**CIS Control 14 — Security Awareness and Skills Training**
- **Safeguard 14.1:** Establish a security awareness program. Microsoft 365 includes Attack Simulator for phishing training. KnowBe4 and Proofpoint Security Awareness Training are cost-effective options.
- **Safeguard 14.2:** Train all staff to recognize phishing and social engineering — the #1 attack vector against accounting firms.
- **Safeguard 14.3:** Train on authentication best practices (why MFA matters, how to recognize MFA fatigue attacks).
- **Safeguard 14.4/14.5:** Train on data handling — what client data can be emailed, how to securely share documents.

**CIS Control 17 — Incident Response Management**
- **Safeguard 17.1:** Designate the IT person (and a partner as backup) to manage security incidents.
- **Safeguard 17.2:** Document contact information for reporting — your cyber insurance carrier, the IRS Stakeholder Liaison (for tax data breaches), state attorney general (for breach notification).
- **Safeguard 17.3/17.4:** Write a basic incident response plan. A one-page runbook covering: detect → contain → notify → recover is sufficient at this stage.

---

**CIS Control 15 — Service Provider Management**
- **Safeguard 15.1:** List all your service providers (cloud accounting vendor, M365/Microsoft, payroll processor, any IT contractors).
- **Safeguard 15.2:** Document a service provider management policy.
- **Safeguard 15.3/15.4:** Classify providers by risk level and confirm security requirements are addressed in contracts (look for data processing agreements, SOC 2 reports from your vendors).

---

## 4. IG2 Priorities to Layer In (After IG1 is Established)

Once IG1 is in place — realistically 3–6 months for a part-time IT resource — prioritize these IG2 additions given your risk profile:

| Priority | Safeguard | Reason for This Firm |
|----------|-----------|----------------------|
| **Immediate** | 6.3 — MFA for externally-exposed apps | Cloud apps accessible from internet; BEC is top threat for accountants |
| **Immediate** | 6.4 — MFA for remote network access | Remote work is common; VPN without MFA is insufficient |
| **High** | 3.11 — Encrypt sensitive data at rest | Client tax/financial data must be encrypted on laptops and file shares |
| **High** | 3.6 — Encrypt data on end-user devices | Enable BitLocker (Windows) or FileVault (Mac) on all devices |
| **High** | 11.3 — Protect recovery data | Backups must be isolated from production to survive ransomware |
| **High** | 9.5 — Implement DMARC enforcement | Move DMARC policy from `p=none` to `p=quarantine` or `p=reject` |
| **Medium** | 7.6 — Automated vulnerability scans | Use Microsoft Secure Score or Tenable Nessus Essentials |
| **Medium** | 8.5 — Collect detailed audit logs | Enable Unified Audit Log in M365 with 1-year retention |
| **Medium** | 12.7 — Remote access VPN | Require VPN for access to on-premises resources |
| **Medium** | 15.5 — Assess service providers | Request SOC 2 Type 2 reports annually from cloud accounting vendor |

---

## 5. Quick Win Summary (Do These This Week)

1. **Enable MFA** for all Microsoft 365 accounts — takes 30 minutes, prevents ~99% of credential attacks.
2. **Audit and remove** all inactive and former-employee accounts in M365 and accounting software.
3. **Verify backups** are running and test restoration from at least one backup.
4. **Configure SPF, DKIM, DMARC** for your email domain — free, takes 1–2 hours.
5. **Enable Microsoft Defender** on all endpoints and confirm it is reporting to M365 Defender portal.
6. **Check for end-of-life software** — any Windows 10 machines should be upgraded before October 2025 end-of-support.

## 7. Regulatory Context

As an accounting firm, your CIS Controls implementation supports compliance with:

- **IRS Publication 4557 / FTC Safeguards Rule (16 CFR Part 314):** Requires a written information security plan (WISP). IG1 + IG2 implementation provides the technical controls underpinning a compliant WISP.
- **State CPA board requirements:** Many states require reasonable security measures for client data.
- **AICPA SOC 2 (if applicable):** If you seek a SOC 2 report, IG2 implementation maps directly to the Security Trust Services Criteria (CC6–CC9).

# CIS Controls Implementation Group Recommendation
## 75-Person Accounting Firm Security Assessment

---

## Recommended Implementation Group: IG1

**You should target CIS Controls Implementation Group 1 (IG1).**

### Why IG1 Is the Right Fit

The CIS Controls define three Implementation Groups based on organizational risk profile, resources, and security maturity:

| Factor | Your Organization | IG Match |
|--------|------------------|----------|
| Organization size | 75 employees | IG1 |
| IT staffing | Part-time, single person | IG1 |
| Security program maturity | No formal assessments | IG1 |
| Data sensitivity | Client financial/tax data | IG1–IG2 boundary |
| Technology environment | Cloud-based SaaS + M365 | IG1 |

IG1 is designed for organizations with limited cybersecurity expertise and resources. It covers the 56 "essential cyber hygiene" safeguards that every organization should have regardless of size — the baseline below which no organization should fall. CIS describes IG1 as protecting against the most common, non-targeted attacks.

**Important nuance:** Your processing of sensitive client financial and tax data pushes your *risk* toward IG2 territory, but your *resources and capacity* clearly place you at IG1 right now. Start with IG1 fully implemented before considering IG2 expansion. Regulatory obligations (IRS Publication 4557, FTC Safeguards Rule for tax preparers) reinforce the urgency of getting IG1 right.

---

## Where to Start: Priority IG1 Safeguards

IG1 spans CIS Controls 1–16 (with specific safeguards per control). Given your profile, prioritize in this order:

### Phase 1: Immediate Actions (Month 1–2)

**CIS Control 5 — Account Management**
- Safeguard 5.3: Disable dormant accounts within 30 days
- Safeguard 5.4: Restrict administrator privileges — your IT person and no one else should have admin rights
- Safeguard 5.6: Centralize account management (M365 Active Directory/Entra ID)

*Why first:* Credential compromise is the #1 entry point for accounting firm breaches. Former employees with active accounts and over-privileged users are immediate risks.

**CIS Control 6 — Access Control Management**
- Safeguard 6.3: Require MFA for all users accessing cloud applications
- Safeguard 6.5: Require MFA for all administrative access

*Why first:* MFA alone blocks over 99% of automated credential attacks. Your M365 environment has MFA built in — this is a configuration task, not a purchase.

**CIS Control 4 — Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets**
- Safeguard 4.1: Establish and maintain a secure configuration process
- Safeguard 4.2: Establish and maintain a secure configuration for network infrastructure
- Apply Microsoft Secure Score baselines for M365

### Phase 2: Core Hygiene (Month 2–4)

**CIS Control 1 — Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets**
- Safeguard 1.1: Maintain a detailed inventory of all enterprise assets
- Know every device that accesses client data

**CIS Control 2 — Inventory and Control of Software Assets**
- Safeguard 2.1: Maintain an inventory of all authorized software
- Safeguard 2.5: Allowlist authorized software on endpoints

**CIS Control 3 — Data Protection**
- Safeguard 3.3: Configure data access control lists — who can access which client files?
- Safeguard 3.11: Encrypt sensitive data at rest on laptops/workstations
- Safeguard 3.12: Segment data processing and storage based on sensitivity

*Why this matters for you:* Client tax data is a high-value target. Data protection controls directly address your regulatory exposure under the FTC Safeguards Rule.

**CIS Control 11 — Data Recovery**
- Safeguard 11.1: Establish and maintain a data recovery process
- Safeguard 11.2: Perform automated backups — verify your cloud accounting software and M365 backups are actually working
- Safeguard 11.4: Test backup recovery quarterly

### Phase 3: Detection and Response Foundation (Month 4–6)

**CIS Control 8 — Audit Log Management**
- Safeguard 8.2: Collect audit logs from M365, cloud accounting software, and network devices
- Safeguard 8.5: Enable Microsoft Defender audit logging

**CIS Control 9 — Email and Web Browser Protections**
- Safeguard 9.1: Use only fully supported browsers and email clients
- Safeguard 9.2: Use DNS filtering services (Cisco Umbrella, Cloudflare Gateway — both have free/low-cost tiers)
- Safeguard 9.5: Enable anti-phishing controls in M365 (Defender for Office 365)

*Why critical for accounting firms:* Phishing and business email compromise (BEC) targeting accounting firms is rampant, especially during tax season. BEC attacks impersonate partners to redirect client payments.

**CIS Control 14 — Security Awareness and Skills Training**
- Safeguard 14.1: Establish and maintain a security awareness program
- Safeguard 14.2: Train employees to recognize social engineering attacks
- Safeguard 14.6: Train employees on how to identify and report phishing

*Practical approach:* Microsoft 365 Business Premium includes Attack Simulator for phishing training. KnowBe4 and Proofpoint offer SMB-appropriate pricing.

**CIS Control 17 — Incident Response Management**
- Safeguard 17.1: Designate personnel to manage incident handling — even if it's your part-time IT person
- Safeguard 17.2: Establish and maintain contact information for reporting security incidents (IRS, state tax agencies, clients)
- Safeguard 17.3: Create a simple written incident response plan

## Practical Considerations for Your Situation

### Leverage What You Already Have
Your Microsoft 365 subscription likely includes significant security tooling at no additional cost:
- **Microsoft Defender Antivirus** — ensure it is active on all endpoints
- **Microsoft Entra ID** (formerly Azure AD) — MFA, conditional access, device compliance
- **Microsoft Defender for Office 365** (Plan 1 included in M365 Business Premium) — anti-phishing, safe links, safe attachments
- **Microsoft Purview** — data loss prevention to prevent client data from leaving via email
- **Microsoft Secure Score** — provides a dashboard showing your current security posture and prioritized recommendations

Check which M365 plan you have. Upgrading from Business Basic/Standard to Business Premium (~$22/user/month) unlocks substantially more security capability and is likely cost-justified given the client data you hold.

### Regulatory Baseline You Must Meet
As an accounting firm handling tax data:
- **IRS Publication 4557** (Safeguarding Taxpayer Data) — mandatory for tax preparers; maps closely to IG1
- **FTC Safeguards Rule** — applies to financial institutions including tax preparers; requires a written information security program, risk assessment, and designated security coordinator
- **State-level data breach notification laws** — know your obligations if client data is compromised

Your IG1 implementation will substantially address these requirements.

### Resource-Constrained Implementation Strategy

Given a part-time IT resource, be realistic:

1. **Use M365 Secure Score as your roadmap** — it prioritizes actions by impact and difficulty
2. **Automate where possible** — Conditional Access policies in Entra ID enforce MFA without manual intervention
3. **Consider a one-time engagement** with an MSSP (Managed Security Service Provider) or CIS-certified assessor to baseline your current state — a 2–3 day assessment will reveal your highest risks
4. **Prioritize prevention over detection** at this stage — MFA, patching, and email filtering prevent incidents that your part-time IT person does not have capacity to investigate

### 90-Day Quick Win Checklist

- [ ] Enable MFA for all M365 users (Entra ID Conditional Access)
- [ ] Remove local administrator rights from standard user accounts
- [ ] Audit and disable inactive accounts
- [ ] Review your M365 Secure Score and address top 10 recommendations
- [ ] Confirm automated backups are running and test restoration
- [ ] Enable Microsoft Defender on all endpoints
- [ ] Enable anti-phishing policies in Defender for Office 365
- [ ] Document a one-page incident response contact list
- [ ] Conduct one phishing awareness training session
- [ ] Create an asset inventory (spreadsheet of all devices and software is sufficient to start)

## Summary

| Recommendation | Detail |
|---------------|--------|
| Target IG | **IG1 (all 56 safeguards)** |
| Start here | **CIS Control 5 (Accounts) and Control 6 (MFA)** |
| Highest risk | Credential compromise, phishing/BEC, unencrypted client data on endpoints |
| Quick wins | MFA in M365, admin privilege restriction, M365 Secure Score review |
| Regulatory anchor | IRS Pub 4557, FTC Safeguards Rule |
| Timeline to IG1 completion | 6–12 months with part-time IT resource |

Completing IG1 will put you ahead of the majority of firms your size and will provide a defensible security posture if a breach occurs. Once IG1 is fully implemented and documented, reassess whether your client obligations and growth trajectory warrant moving to IG2.

# CIS Controls v8 IG2 Gap Assessment
## Manufacturing Company — 350 Employees, IT Team of 5

## Step 1: Implementation Group Determination

**Profile:**

| Factor | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| Size | 350 employees |
| IT Capability | 5-person dedicated IT team; responsible for managing and protecting IT infrastructure |
| Data Sensitivity | Manufacturing environment — likely contains proprietary process data, supplier/customer records, OT/IT boundary considerations |
| Risk Tolerance | Operational disruptions would impact production and revenue; some outages tolerable but sustained downtime costly |
| Regulatory Exposure | Possible CMMC/DFARS exposure if defense supplier; EHS data; financial records |

**Determination: IG2**

This organization clearly meets IG2 criteria: it has dedicated IT personnel responsible for managing and protecting IT, stores data that could affect operations if compromised, and can withstand some outage. IG3 is not required as there is no evidence of a dedicated security team (separate from IT) or significant regulatory oversight of sensitive data. All IG1 and IG2 safeguards apply.

**Known Implemented Controls:**
- Antivirus on all endpoints
- Monthly Windows patching
- Basic perimeter firewall
- Annual security awareness training

**Known Gaps:**
- No MFA on VPN
- No vulnerability scanner
- No centralized log management (only Windows Event Viewer per server)

| | 15.6 Monitor service providers | IG2 | Not implemented | No ongoing vendor monitoring | HIGH |
| **16: Application Software Security** | 16.1 Secure development process | IG2 | Unknown — manufacturing context | Likely not applicable if no in-house dev; confirm and document | LOW |
| | 16.2 Process for software vulnerability reports | IG2 | Unknown | No vulnerability disclosure intake process | MEDIUM |
| | 16.7 Use hardening configuration templates | IG2 | Unknown | CIS Benchmark hardening for deployed applications not confirmed | MEDIUM |
| **17: Incident Response Management** | 17.1 Designate incident response personnel | IG1 | Unknown | No formal IR team or designated roles confirmed | HIGH |
| | 17.3 Enterprise incident reporting process | IG1 | Unknown | No documented incident reporting process | HIGH |
| | 17.4 Establish incident response process | IG1 | Unknown | No IR plan or playbooks confirmed | HIGH |
| | 17.7 Conduct IR exercises | IG2 | Not implemented | No tabletop or IR drills | HIGH |
| | 17.9 Establish incident thresholds | IG2 | Not implemented | No defined thresholds for what constitutes a security incident | MEDIUM |
| **18: Penetration Testing** | 18.1 Establish penetration testing program | IG2 | Not implemented | No pen testing program | MEDIUM |
| | 18.2 Perform periodic external pen tests | IG2 | Not implemented | No external pen tests conducted | HIGH |
| | 18.3 Remediate pen test findings | IG2 | N/A — no tests conducted | Dependent on 18.2 | MEDIUM |
